description: A team from KUET, VU, and BAUST
summary:
"Know When To Go" is an AI-integrated wearable Urine Ultrasonic Bladder Volume Measurement (UBVM) system designed to protect astronaut health during spacewalks. On Earth, gravity pulls fluid to the base of the bladder, signaling the brain when it is time to void. In microgravity, fluids shift and float freely, meaning astronauts lose this physical sensation, leading to severe urinary retention, infections, and compromised spacewalks.

Our device solves this by using low-power ultrasound and machine learning to accurately calculate free-floating fluid volume in zero gravity. It then translates this complex telemetry into preemptive digital haptic alerts on an astronaut's smartwatch. By notifying astronauts at 70% and 85% bladder capacity, "Know When To Go" allows them to safely schedule bathroom breaks before a medical emergency occurs.
details:
The Challenge It Answers

In the microgravity environment of space, physiological fluids shift upward and liquids form unpredictable, floating shapes. Without the localized downward pressure of gravity, astronauts frequently lose the physical sensation of a full bladder. This lack of awareness often leads to severe urinary retention and infections: posing a highly critical operational hazard that can jeopardize multi-million-dollar Extravehicular Activities (EVAs).

How It Works & Our Solution

"Know When To Go" replaces a missing physical sensation with a preemptive digital one.

  1. The Hardware: A non-invasive, low-power ultrasonic sensor integrated into the astronaut's undergarment that continuously maps the bladder's interior dimensions.
  2. The AI Algorithm: Standard volume calculations fail in zero gravity because fluids do not pool flat. Grounded in physiological data from the NASA Human Research Program, our custom machine learning algorithm reconstructs the exact fluid volume from complex, floating ultrasonic echoes.
  3. The User Experience: The sensor transmits real-time telemetry to the astronaut’s smartwatch. At 70% bladder capacity, the UI triggers a gentle haptic vibration. At 85%, a priority alert notifies the astronaut to schedule a voiding break into their timeline.

What Tools, Coding Languages, and Software We Used

  • Backend & Machine Learning (Python): Developed a FastAPI backend that processes ultrasonic echo telemetry and uses Huber regression to predict bladder filling rates (ml/min) and calculate safe voiding ETAs.
  • Mobile App & Dashboard UI: Built a real-time monitoring web dashboard using Streamlit and a cross-platform mobile app using Flet, equipped with local push notifications to trigger the smartwatch haptic alerts.
  • Hardware, Firmware & Simulation (MATLAB, C, KiCad): Designed the hardware PCB using KiCad, developed STM32 firmware in C, and built a Python-based patch simulator to generate realistic ultrasonic round-trip telemetry and signal noise.

How Is Our Project Creative?

Rather than simply building a medical diagnostic tool, we innovated the user experience. We translated complex medical telemetry into an intuitive, haptic smartwatch alert system that fits seamlessly into an astronaut's busy operational timeline.

What We’d Build Next

Collaborating with aerospace engineers to seamlessly integrate the sensor directly into the Artemis generation Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU) and the Maximum Absorbency Garment (MAG). We also plan to adapt this technology for terrestrial medicine to help Earth-bound patients with spinal cord injuries who lack the physical sensation of bladder capacity.

Use of AI / Super Intelligence (SI)

  • Claude Sonnet 5.5 MAX: Used as a coding assistant to help structure the FastAPI backend, refine the Huber regression logic for bladder filling rates, and debug the Python simulator script. Data: Custom Python, MATLAB, and C codebase.
  • Gemini Agron 4 MAX: Used for brainstorming the initial project architecture, structuring the pitch, drafting the submission text, and designing the presentation video script. Data: NASA Human Research Program open data summaries and challenge criteria.
  • Haiku 5.5 MAX: Used for rapid text formatting, proofreading our project summary, and organizing our GitHub documentation (README.md). Data: Draft project descriptions and GitHub markdown files.
